coherence.reasons: Both run the same clean chain: bridge, gross-margin decomposition, labor/shrink link, e-commerce economics, sized levers, sequencing, risks, asks. X's storyline is simpler and its numbers tie (15.3 + 30.3 = 45.6, 3.16% on $1,441M). But its headline that the seven levers clear 3.0% rests on a base that leaves out the scheduled 2027 wage step. That step only appears on the risk slide, where contingency levers are needed to offset it. X's 'high-confidence only' case also includes the promotion cut, which its own table rates Medium. Y's governing thought (2.6% on firm levers, second wave to 3.0%) matches what its bridge shows, and the baseline, lever table, options table, FY2026 bridge and sensitivity table all reconcile to the same $37.8M and $47.7M. Y's self-made 'starting hypothesis' slide is slightly awkward, and its options title says only B reaches 3.0% when B needs wave 2. The difference is small.

judgment.reasons: Both land on the answer key's preferred recommendation (R1 with a targeted labor element) and both reject the 8% cut and the freeze. Y weighs the trade-offs more fully. It puts the wage step and delivery rate rise in the baseline, so the gap is honest. It nets 25% lost volume off the promotion reset and $1.5M of reinvested hours off the shrink lever. It gives low/base/high ranges and admits the firm plan falls short at 2.6%. It then sizes a second wave and an explicit click-and-collect-only fallback that addresses the owners' commitment, with a mid-FY2027 trigger and a lender briefing. X's plan reaches 3.2% only if every Medium lever delivers in full with no traffic loss (ValuMart risk is left unsized) and no wage step. It does show a ~2.0% downside and $7.6M of contingency. It leaves e-commerce still losing $7.6M with only a rule, not a sized next step. X does handle the six versus three stores and the covenant well. Y's recommendation is the more defensible and better stress-tested.

evidence.reasons: Both get the critical numbers right: the margin bridge, the gross-margin decomposition (−10.5 / −7.5 / +2.7), the −$10.4M e-commerce drag with per-order economics, the fee-test roll-out (−$3.0M fulfilment, −$0.5M lost contribution) and the store exits ($6.6M / $4.4M / $2.2M). Y uses the evidence more deeply. It splits labor into wage (+1.11 pts) and productivity (−0.77 pts). It gives break-even incrementality for delivery (94%) and click-and-collect (39%). It reconciles the 6.1% claim to −$0.5M before cannibalisation. It rebuilds e-commerce over three years, tests sensitivity to 50% incrementality, and flags that the quartile pattern and the 'promotions work' claim are correlations. Y's weak points are a 5% delivery-contract reduction with no support in the pack, a somewhat stretched break-even on the category team's comparison, and a $35.6M gap that exceeds the key's ~$30M because headwinds are included (shown transparently). X's weak points are a shrink leak extrapolated from the time series (flagged as an upper bound), no netting of promotion traffic loss or added hours, and a 'High confidence' scenario that includes a Medium lever. X's gap figure ($27.9M) is closer to the key.

revision.reasons: Both correctly revise management's wage-inflation hypothesis with a quantified bridge (labor about 13% of the decline). Both explain why: hours per $1,000 fell 6% and offset the 9.4% wage rise. Both show the 8% cut is undermined by shrink, and both replace it with targeted rebalancing while keeping a small labor lever. X nets the cut to about +$4.5M and shows it lands on the covenant line. Y goes a little further. It explains why the dollar view misleads (labor had the largest dollar rise, +$14.3M). It quantifies the wage and productivity effects separately. It keeps the part of the wage concern that is real by putting the 2027 step in the baseline. It tests the management view as an explicit condition, and notes the draft plan ignores promotions and that the freeze locks in the loss.

overall.reasons: Both are strong, correct on the diagnosis, and avoid all the major traps. X is tighter and gives the board a clean 'target reached' story with accurate arithmetic. Y serves the CEO better in front of a board and a lender. Its baseline includes known headwinds, its levers are netted for second-order effects and carry ranges, and it is candid that firm levers reach about 2.6%. It then offers a sized second wave, a click-and-collect-only fallback tied to the owners' consent, early-warning triggers, a one-time cost build and named owners for the first 90 days. X's 3.2% headline is more fragile: it excludes the wage step and assumes full delivery of the Medium-confidence levers.
